messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Michael Hargrove, a 55-year-old single European American counselor, described a life that had narrowed around one evening at a community center where he had volunteered after work. During a heated dispute in the hallway, someone hurled a chair and a plastic bin across the room, and the sudden crash was followed by the sharp, burnt smell of an overheated electrical panel and the unmistakable odor of smoke drifting in from a small fire that had started behind a wall. Michael had been close enough to see people bolt for the exits, and though the fire was contained quickly, the chaos lodged in him as a man-made disaster that felt both sudden and absurdly close. In the weeks after, he found himself avoiding friends because invitations to dinner, bars, or even someone’s apartment brought him too near conversation about “that night,” and he had come to dread any setting where he might have to think about it. He also monitored his own thoughts with grim vigilance, checking constantly for signs that he was “going crazy,” because the event had left him convinced that if he let his mind wander toward it, he would not be able to handle what came next.  

What Michael noticed first was how his body seemed to betray him. He would catch a whiff of burnt toast from a neighbor’s kitchen or smoke from a passing truck and feel his chest tighten before he had time to tell himself he was safe. If someone nearby slammed a mug down, tossed a coat across a chair, or threw a set of keys onto a desk, his stomach lurched and he would scan the room for an exit without fully deciding to do so. Those cues pulled up more than alarm; they carried the event back into him in fragments. Sometimes, when he tried not to think about it, he would still be flooded by the same raw terror he had felt in the hallway, but without any clear picture of the faces, the room, or the sequence of what had happened. At other times he would suddenly smell smoke or singed wiring in his mind as vividly as if it were in front of him. The memory itself felt oddly detached, as if it belonged to another man entirely, someone he had watched rather than lived as himself. Because the sensations arrived so abruptly and stripped of context, Michael became more certain that his body was still reacting as if danger were present, and that the world could turn on him again without warning.  

That conviction did not stay abstract. Each time a smell or a thrown object jolted him, the memory came back stronger and more bodily, and the more it came back, the more threatening it felt. He began to think he had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, and he interpreted every flare of panic as evidence that something was still wrong inside him. The more he braced himself against those moments, the more he felt trapped in the memory’s emotional intensity, especially when it rose without any image at all, leaving him shaken and ashamed in his office after a session or in the parking lot after work. He tried to avoid thinking about the event altogether, telling himself that even one deliberate effort to remember would overwhelm him, yet that avoidance offered little relief. Instead, the memory seemed to return in the background, shaped by the very effort to push it away, and he found himself watching his own mind for signs of breakdown with almost the same intensity that he watched doorways and hallways for danger.  

Over months, the pattern spread into his life as a counselor. Michael could still sit with clients, but after sessions he became reluctant to join colleagues for lunch, and he turned down long-standing plans with friends because he feared the casual talk might drift toward fires, violence, or “stressful experiences.” At home he avoided cooking when there was any chance of a burnt smell, and he kept windows open even in cold weather if he thought he might catch a whiff of smoke. Objects thrown in frustration—someone slapping a file onto a desk, a client tossing a pen, a neighbor throwing a bag into a dumpster—would spike him into the same unease that had first followed the disaster. Each time, he felt the old memory stir, and each time that stirred fear seemed to confirm his belief that his body was unreliable and that he remained on the edge of catastrophe. In that way his vigilance and his efforts to keep the event out of mind only kept the sensations alive, and the sensations kept convincing him that danger was still near. By the time he sought help, he was exhausted by the loop of smells, thrown objects, and internal monitoring, and he said what frightened him most was not only the memory itself but the fear that if he kept living this way, he would lose confidence in his own mind and his ability to remain the calm, competent man his work had always required.
